events.title: Plata announces $1 billion ARR milestone
events.reason: Every claim is backed by the sources. The PR Newswire release dated 19 Oct 2026, later corrected, gives: $1B ARR in September 2026; under 3.5 years since the April 2023 launch; under a year after the banking license; fastest digital bank (company's assessment); 4M+ customers; fourth credit card issuer by customers; only full-suite digital bank; Mexico profitability within 6 months; and a corrected boilerplate. Oninvest reports the CEO's Bloomberg interview the same day: $85M of September revenue, profitability next year, and Bloomberg's figures of about 8 years for Nu and 6 for Revolut. The announcement happened on 19 Oct, inside the window. Revenue scale, profitability timing and valuation context bear directly on a share purchase.

events.title: Reported $5 billion valuation and large private funding
events.reason: The description misstates the sources in three ways. First, it says dates and investors are not given, but Oninvest says Plata raised $405M in April 2026 from Bicycle Capital, QIA and BTG Pactual, with a related article dated 16.04.2026. Second, it calls Plata 'the most valuable' private player, while the source says 'one of the highest' among Latin American private fintechs. Third, it treats $405M vs $300M as conflicting figures, but the $300M is a separate June credit facility from Oaktree and Macquarie (CB Insights' 'Line of Credit - III'). Because the sources date the funding and valuation to April 2026, a null date is not justified, and the event falls before the Oct 17–Nov 16 window. Plata's valuation and funding are directly relevant to discussing a share purchase.

events.title: Expansion to Colombia and exploration of further markets
events.reason: Every claim is backed by the sources. Plata launched in Colombia at the beginning of September 2026, with no exact day given. Oninvest says Plata is exploring a launch in Brazil and that management sees Argentina and Peru as potentially attractive. Pulse 2.0 says Plata presents its in-house technology, banking license and product portfolio as the foundation for regional expansion. A null date is correct because the sources give only 'beginning of September'. That timing is still clear enough to place the Colombia launch before the 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-16 window, so it is out of window. The geographic expansion strategy is relevant to valuing the growth case for buying shares.

events.title: Banco Plata begins operating as a full bank in Mexico; credit-card and deposit growth
events.reason: The source supports that Banco Plata began operating as a full-service bank in March, that its credit-card portfolio grew from MXN12.8bn to almost MXN19.0bn between March and August, that this was 60% of Nubank's portfolio, and that deposits reached MXN25.9bn ($1.4bn). It does not mention Nubank's MXN 31 billion figure or regulator data, so the description is not fully supported. A null date is acceptable because only the month is given, not an exact day. March 2026 through August falls before the Oct 17 to Nov 16 2026 research window. Banking status, loan-book growth and deposit funding bear directly on a discussion about buying shares.

events.title: Revolut launches full banking operations in Mexico
events.reason: The source supports every statement: Revolut launched full banking operations in Mexico in January 2026, Nu and MercadoLibre remain the largest fintechs, and Plata has become a major lending competitor. The source gives only the month, not the day, so a null date is acceptable. The event is about Revolut, not Plata. It happened in January 2026, before the research window. It is only competitive-landscape context for a Plata share purchase.

goal.reason: The questions are specific and well suited to buying bank shares. They cover whether shares are actually available and in what form, valuation provenance and conflicting figures, the ARR definition, conflicting profitability timelines, card-book credit quality, expansion dilution and foreign-ownership regulatory approvals. Weaknesses: the last five 'discussion points' read as source annotations ('This shows…', 'This is the main…') with unclear referents, and they largely repeat the questions rather than adding new points. events.title: Pop Mart shares hit 18-month low after Q3 disclosure; analysts cut estimates
events.reason: The sources support every claim in the event. Pop Mart reported Q3 results late Tuesday (filed Oct 27), and shares fell as much as 6% to HK$123.8, an 18-month low, on Wednesday Oct 28. Jefferies cut its 2027-28 estimates by 9-12% after results came in weaker than its forecast 30% decline. The COO cited a high base effect. The BBC reports shares are down more than 50% from last year's peak, and Labubu releases are trading below retail. Oct 28 falls inside the research window. Weakening demand and a falling share price bear directly on Pop Mart's appetite for new stores and its standing as a tenant in lease talks.

events.title: Pop Mart discloses Q3 2026 revenue down 45%-50% year on year
events.reason: The sources confirm the Hong Kong Stock Exchange filing on 27 October (local time). They confirm the 45-50% total decline and every regional range. The 23.8% first-half growth is also stated. Chosun Biz says the company poured funds into finding the next hit but failed to fill the gap. A source's hat tips cite Bloomberg (Oct. 27) confirming the Q3 figures. The S2/S5 labels could not be checked against the source texts, but every content claim is supported. The event falls inside the research window. It bears directly on a retail lease: sources note that over-expansion into prime stores with heavy fixed rents strained Pop Mart's finances, which affects tenant risk and lease terms.

events.title: Pop Mart's new Oxford Street (London) flagship scheduled to open
events.reason: The source supports each factual claim: the 19 Oct article, the Instagram announcement, the 10 am Friday 23 October opening at 149-151 Oxford Street, the exclusive products and activities, the Charing Cross Road store as the 16th UK shop, the missing size/rent/staffing figures and the Miniso/HMV building deal. Calling it the 'former' HMV building is a minor inference. The 23 Oct date is only the planned opening, and the sources do not confirm the opening happened. That makes date_ok false and leaves in_window unknown, even though the planned date falls inside the window. The event is about Pop Mart and its active store expansion on a prime street, so it bears directly on a discussion about leasing retail space to the brand.

events.title: Pop Mart expands into theme parks and experiences (POP LAND, Monsterland)
events.reason: Every statement in the description matches the sources. Blooloop (30 Oct 2026) covers POP LAND as the base for expansion, the search for partners, and Monsterland as a 2026 Labubu expansion with no opening date. SEE News mentions the Beijing theme park and film plans. Chosun Biz mentions Twinkle Twinkle, Dimoo and Pop Bakery Singapore. The sources give no single date for this ongoing expansion: POP LAND opened in 2023 and Monsterland is only dated '2026', so a null date is correct and in_window is unknown. The publication date alone does not place the event in the window. For a retail-space lease meeting this is useful background: McManus mentions partnerships bringing Pop Mart retail and entertainment into public spaces. It does not bear directly on store leasing.

goal.reason: The questions are specific and tied to the leasing goal. They cover store format (flagship vs. smaller), lease structure (fixed vs. turnover rent, break options, incentives), space and layout needs for experiential elements, location and co-tenancy criteria, covenant strength, and the approval timeline. Several draw on concrete context such as Oxford Street, the COO's 'stable development phase' comment and Miniso's competition for prime sites, which makes them actionable. Weaknesses: the last four items are background notes that largely repeat the earlier questions rather than adding new discussion points. The list leans on a European 'Q3 decline of -50% to -55%' figure that should be verified, since it may be a quarter-on-quarter rather than year-on-year comparison and could set a misleading negotiating premise. A few questions, such as the IP-dependence one, invite general corporate strategy answers rather than terms specific to our space.

facts.fact: Kellogg's changed the UK recipe of Rice Krispies and Coco Pops (corn and rice flour instead of whole rice grains), citing weather-hit grain supplies, and admitted the 'snap, crackle and pop' may be quieter after customer complaints.

source.title: Kellogg's admits snap, crackle and pop is quieter after uproar over Rice Krispies recipe change

facts.reason: The briefing covers the UK reformulation of Rice Krispies and Coco Pops: rice flour, and a rice and corn flour blend, replacing whole rice grains. It also covers the attribution to weather affecting grain quality and availability, and the customer complaints, including a review saying the cereal no longer crackles. It does not say that Kellogg's itself admitted the 'snap, crackle and pop' may be quieter.

events.title: WK Kellogg Co. clarifies that North American Rice Krispies are unchanged
events.reason: All three sources confirm that a WK Kellogg Co. spokesperson said the U.S. and Canadian Rice Krispies, Cocoa Krispies and Frosted Krispies are unchanged and made with real rice. CTV places the statement on Wednesday, Nov 4, 2026, which falls inside the research window. CTV and Fox note that Kellanova/Mars operates the brands outside North America. The event concerns the Kellogg's brand itself. It is useful background on the brand and on how Kellogg's is now split between owners, but it does not directly bear on a collaboration.

events.title: Kellogg's confirms the UK recipe change for Rice Krispies and Coco Pops
events.reason: The core facts are supported by the sources: the whole-rice swap to rice flour (plus corn flour in Coco Pops), the weather rationale, the taste/texture assessment and listening to consumer feedback, unchanged fat/salt/sugar status, no artificial additives, unchanged fibre, vitamin D and iron, and the 'may contain' to 'contains wheat gluten' label change. However, the description says the Tuesday date comes from the BBC and CBC texts and their 2026-11-04 publication dates. The BBC text mentions no 'Tuesday' and gives no publication date ('6 days ago'). Under strict evaluation that misattribution counts as an unsupported statement. The date itself holds up: CBC says the UK spokesperson gave its statement on Tuesday, BNN says UK outlets reported it Tuesday, and UA.News published on 3 Nov 2026, which is a Tuesday. That date falls inside the window. The event concerns the Kellogg's brand (UK, run by Kellanova/Mars). For a collaboration meeting it is useful background on supply pressures, reformulation and consumer backlash, but it does not directly affect a partnership.

events.title: UK consumer backlash over the changed Rice Krispies and Coco Pops
events.reason: Two statements in the description are false. The second outlet (East Kilbride Today/Newsquest) is not a one-line summary: it is a full article with quoted complaints and a Kellogg's statement. The sources also do give complaint dates, contrary to the description: embedded X posts are dated October 20, 2026 (Coco Pops) and October 21, 2026 (Rice Krispies). Because those dates establish when the backlash occurred, leaving the date null is wrong. The backlash ran from about October 20 to October 29, 2026, which is inside the research window. The event concerns Kellogg's own UK brands. It is useful background on brand reputation and on the recipe changes Kellogg's attributes to supply pressures, but it does not bear directly on a collaboration.

events.title: Ownership split of the Kellogg's businesses (context)
events.reason: The sources support every claim. Fox Business reports the 2023 split into Kellanova (Kellogg's brands outside North America) and WK Kellogg Co. (North American cereal), with Ferrero acquiring WK Kellogg Co. in September 2025 and Mars acquiring Kellanova in December 2025. BBC likewise says Kellanova is owned by Mars and WK Kellogg's was taken over by Ferrero. This is a composite background item with no single event date; its parts are dated only to a year (2023) or a month, so null is reasonable. All of these events predate the research window. Knowing which entity and parent company own which Kellogg's business is important for approaching a collaboration.

events.title: Climate pressure is driving reformulation across food and drink
events.reason: The article supports every statement: FoodNavigator places Kellogg's reformulation within a wider trend, says climate pressures are increasingly driving reformulation across food and drink, and says cocoa and orange juice suppliers are adapting recipes. The trend has no specific event date in the source (only the 04-Nov-2026 publication date), so the null date is appropriate and timing is unknown. The event is about an industry-wide trend, with the cocoa (Pladis) and orange juice (Kerry) examples, rather than Kellogg's itself. Kellogg's appears only as context. It is useful industry background for a collaboration discussion but has limited direct bearing on the meeting goal.

goal.reason: Specific and well grounded: the points name concrete entities (Kellanova/Mars Snacking vs WK Kellogg Co./Ferrero), products (Rice Krispies, Coco Pops), issues (rice supply risk, wheat gluten allergen change, UK consumer reaction) and a relevant market (Italy). Confirming the correct entity and decision-makers first is genuinely useful. Weaknesses: the discussion points largely repeat the questions; several read as article analysis ('It shows...') referring to an unseen source rather than meeting talking points; nothing is tailored to what our side offers; and practical collaboration items (scope, timelines, commercial model, next steps) are missing.

events.title: Bending Spoons seeks $1.5 billion in debt to fund acquisitions
events.reason: The description wrongly says pricing and terms are not stated. The source gives them: $1B of five-year senior secured notes in the low 10% area, a $500M-equivalent euro tranche in the low 9% area, and expected BB- ratings. The core facts are supported: the $1.5B raise, acquisition funding from portfolio cash and debt, the CEO comment 'this month', and the 61% share gain since the July listing. Leaving the date null is acceptable because the sources give only a publication date, not an exact launch date. The present-tense 'is tapping' in an October 27 article places the offering inside the window. The event is about Bending Spoons and is highly relevant to an investment discussion, as it covers leverage, financing cost and the acquisition strategy.
